To demonstrate the issue and how to deal with it, consider the data in the following table, showing the ages and corresponding weights of five players on a baseball team.

items.title: Interpreting Information From a Scatter Plot

sections.normalized_html:
The scatter plot above shows the relationship between the number of bags of popcorn sold one day and the price per bag at nine locations.

Given that none of the points overlap, which of the following statements are true?

  1. Only one location sold exactly [MATH: 10] bags of popcorn.

  2. Two locations sold bags of popcorn for [MATH: \[math]1.40] each.

  3. No location sold more than [MATH: 30] bags of popcorn.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/1db6081814f3b5c2b488e394c39648bb]

The scatter plot above shows the relationship between the number of bags of popcorn sold one day and the price per bag at nine locations.

Given that none of the points overlap, which of the following statements are true?

1. Only one location sold exactly [MATH: 10] bags of popcorn.
2. Two locations sold bags of popcorn for [MATH: \[math]1.40] each.
3. No location sold more than [MATH: 30] bags of popcorn.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine our scatter plot.

  • Statement I is true. The scatter plot has only one dot whose vertical coordinate equals [MATH: 10,] namely, [MATH: (1.8,10).] This means only one location sold exactly [MATH: 10] bags of popcorn.

  • Statement II is false. The scatter plot has only one dot whose horizontal coordinate equals [MATH: 1.4,] namely, [MATH: (1.4,30).] This means that only one location sold popcorn for [MATH: \[math]1.40] per bag.

  • Statement III is false. From the scatter plot, one location sold more than [MATH: 30] bags of popcorn, represented by the dot above the horizontal line.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
